etymology: A modern term claiming a “gender identity” at variance with one’s biological sex; from the Latin trans, across, and gender.
biblical_def: Transgender is the modern claim that a person’s inward sense of self—a so-called gender identity—may differ from, and override, the biological sex of the body, so that a man may be a woman or a woman a man. The dictionary measures this claim against the Word of God, and finds it a corruption of the doctrine of creation. God created man in His own image; male and female created He them. The Lord Jesus confirmed it: He which made them at the beginning made them male and female. Sex is not an assignment to be revised but a creational, embodied, God-given reality; the body fearfully and wonderfully made declares the Maker’s design, and that soul knows it right well. The dictionary affirms with all earnestness that every person who struggles with the distress of body and self is an image-bearer of God, to be met with truth and compassion, not with cruelty or contempt. But compassion does not lie. The path of bodily mutilation and chemical sterilization in pursuit of an impossible change is not healing but harm against the body and the soul’s good, and the ideology that severs identity from embodied sex is a revolt against Genesis 1:27. The law’s prohibition of cross-dressing witnesses to the goodness of the creational distinction of the sexes. The dictionary reads transgender ideology as a corruption of the imago Dei to be answered with the truth of creation and the mercy of the gospel, which calls all sinners—ourselves first—to find their true self not in self-invention but in Christ.
webster_summary: The modern claim that an inward “gender identity” overrides biological sex; a corruption of the doctrine of creation, answered by the truth that God made man male and female.

corruption_summary: Transgender ideology severs identity from embodied sex, calling a man a woman and revising the body to fit the feeling; it is a corruption of Genesis 1:27 to be answered with creation’s truth and the gospel’s mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name plainly is the ideology of gender identity itself, which teaches that the inward sense of self is the true self and the sexed body a mere outward shell to be altered, hidden, or overruled—so that a man may “identify as” a woman, the categories of “gender assigned at birth” and “gender identity” replacing the creational fact that God made them male and female. This is a direct revolt against Genesis 1:27. Sex is not assigned by a doctor’s observation but given by the Creator and written into every cell; it cannot be changed, only marred. The chemical and surgical attempts to remake the body do not produce the other sex but sterilize and wound a healthy one—harm against the body and against the soul’s good, dressed in the language of care.

The principle to recover is the goodness of the creational distinction of male and female and the true self found in Christ. Every person caught in this confusion bears the image of God and is to be met with both unflinching truth and real compassion—never with mockery or scorn, for we too are sinners saved by grace. But love does not affirm the lie; it tells the truth that the body is fearfully and wonderfully made and that wholeness is found not in self-invention but in repentance and faith. The gospel does not leave any sinner as he is, and it offers to the one in this distress, as to all, a new and true identity in the crucified and risen Lord.

etymology: The holding of persons as property in bondage; from the medieval Latin sclavus, originally of the Slavic peoples taken captive.
biblical_def: Slavery is the holding of human beings as property in bondage, and the dictionary reads the Bible’s treatment of it with care, against both those who use Scripture to justify the chattel slavery of the modern age and those who charge Scripture with endorsing it. The Bible regulated a form of servitude in the ancient world—debt-bondage, indentured service with mandated release, and the condition of war-captives—hedging it with protections unknown to the surrounding nations: the manstealer was to be put to death, the runaway not returned to his master, the servant freed in the sabbatical year. But Scripture condemns outright the very engine of the trans-Atlantic slave trade: he that stealeth a man and selleth him shall surely be put to death, and menstealers are listed among the lawless and ungodly. The kidnapping and sale of Africans was manstealing under sentence of death by God’s own law. More deeply, the gospel sows the seed of slavery’s undoing: in Christ there is neither bond nor free, all one in Him; and Paul sends the runaway Onesimus back to Philemon not now as a servant but as a brother beloved. The dictionary holds that chattel slavery as practiced in the modern West was sin—manstealing and the dishonoring of God’s image-bearers—and that the gospel’s logic of every man a brother in Christ is what at last armed the Christian abolitionists who struck the chains.

corruption_summary: Scripture is twisted both to justify chattel slavery and to indict the Bible as pro-slavery; rightly read, it condemns manstealing under death and sows the gospel seed that undid the trade—every man a brother in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite errors must be answered. The first is the old defense of the trans-Atlantic slave trade by proof-text, which the dictionary flatly refuses: that trade was built on manstealing—the kidnapping and sale of human beings—which God’s law punishes with death and which the apostle names among the works contrary to sound doctrine. The chattel slavery of the modern West, treating image-bearers as breeding stock and merchandise, was sin, and no honest reading of Scripture excuses it. The second error is the modern charge that the Bible simply endorses slavery; but Scripture regulated and hemmed in a far different ancient servitude, forbade the return of the fugitive, and condemned the very kidnapping at the trade’s root.

The principle to recover is the gospel that undid slavery from within. Scripture does not merely tolerate a fallen institution; it plants the seed of its destruction in the great truth that all men are made in God’s image and that in Christ there is neither bond nor free, all one in Him. When Paul sends the runaway Onesimus back to his master, it is no longer as a slave but as a brother beloved—a quiet revolution. It was this gospel logic, that every man is a brother for whom Christ died, that armed Wilberforce and the Christian abolitionists to break the chains, and it is the standard by which the dictionary judges all bondage of man by man.

etymology: The treating of human beings as less than human; from the Latin de-, removal, and humanus, human.
biblical_def: Dehumanization is the sin of regarding and treating a human being as less than human—denying in word, thought, or deed the dignity that belongs to every person as a bearer of the image of God. Scripture grounds the worth of man not in his usefulness, his strength, his stage of development, or his group, but in creation: God made man in His own image, and crowned him with glory and honor, a little lower than the angels. This is why the shedding of innocent blood is so grave—whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for in the image of God made He man—and why the tongue that curses men made after the similitude of God is condemned. To oppress the poor is to reproach his Maker. Every great cruelty of history has begun by first denying the full humanity of its victims: the slave reduced to property, the unborn child reckoned a clump of cells, the aged and disabled judged a burden not worth living, the enemy painted as vermin to be exterminated. The dictionary names dehumanization as a root sin against the imago Dei, and holds up against it the unwavering biblical truth that every human being—born and unborn, strong and weak, friend and foe—bears the image of God and is owed the honor, protection, and love due an image-bearer of the Almighty.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though “dignity” is severed from its ground in the imago Dei; the worth of man rests on creation, and dehumanization is sin against the image of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the ground of human worth. The secular age affirms “human dignity” loudly but cannot account for it, having cut it loose from its only sure foundation—that man is made in the image of God. A dignity grounded merely in usefulness, autonomy, or social consensus is a dignity that can be revoked when a life is judged inconvenient; and so the same age that proclaims human rights dehumanizes the unborn child, the dying, and the disabled when they cost too much. Without the imago Dei, “dignity” is a sentiment with no defense against the strong who would deny it to the weak.

The principle to recover is the image of God as the unshakable ground of every human life’s worth. Man is crowned with glory and honor by his Maker; his blood may not be shed because he is made in God’s image; the tongue may not curse him because he is made in God’s likeness; the poor may not be oppressed because to do so reproaches his Maker. Dehumanization—whether of the slave, the unborn, the enemy, or the outcast—is sin against the Almighty whose image the victim bears. The church honors God by honoring every image-bearer, born and unborn, strong and weak, friend and foe.

etymology: The decline of Christian belief and practice in a formerly Christian society; from de-, removal, and Christian.
biblical_def: Dechristianization is the process by which a society once shaped by the Christian faith loses it—abandoning the worship of God, the authority of His Word, and the moral order of His law, until a culture that was nominally Christian becomes practically pagan. It is the modern West’s great apostasy: nations that once filled churches, swore by Scripture, and ordered their laws and calendars by the gospel now empty the pews, mock the faith, and order life as though God were not. Scripture knows the pattern. After Joshua’s generation died, there arose another generation which knew not the LORD, nor the works He had done for Israel; the fathers’ faith was not transmitted, and the children turned to idols. Where men do not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gives them over to a reprobate mind; a people is destroyed for lack of knowledge; and the day of Christ shall not come except there come a falling away first. Dechristianization is no mere statistical decline but a spiritual judgment and a spiritual battle. The dictionary names it as the apostasy it is—a forsaking of the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns that can hold no water—and answers it not with nostalgia for a lost Christendom but with the only remedy: the faithful preaching of the gospel, the catechizing of the young, and the recovery of the Word, by which alone a dechristianized people can be re-evangelized and revived.

corruption_summary: Dechristianization is dressed up as progress and enlightenment; Scripture names it apostasy and judgment—a forsaking of the living God for broken cisterns—answered by the gospel and the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to name is the secular framing of dechristianization as liberation and progress—the casting off of faith celebrated as a coming-of-age, the emptying of the churches read as enlightenment. But Scripture names the reality differently. A people that forsakes the LORD has committed evil, exchanging the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns that hold no water; a generation that knows not the LORD nor His works has lost a treasure, not gained a freedom; and where men will not retain God in their knowledge, He gives them over to a reprobate mind and a society to its own dissolution. Dechristianization is apostasy and, often, judgment—not a brighter dawn but a deepening dark.

The principle to recover is the only remedy for a dechristianized people. The answer is not a wistful nostalgia for a vanished Christendom, nor a merely political reconquest of the culture, but the same means by which the gospel first conquered: the faithful preaching of Christ crucified, the diligent catechizing of children so that the faith is not lost in a single generation, and the recovery of the authority and sufficiency of the Word. A people is destroyed for lack of knowledge; a people may be revived by it. The church’s task in a dechristianized age is to re-evangelize it, trusting the Spirit who alone can make dry bones live.

etymology: A modern sociological term for those who claim no religious affiliation—who answer “none” when asked their religion.
biblical_def: The “nones” are those who, when asked their religion, answer “none”—the rising multitude of the religiously unaffiliated in the modern West, neither professing the Christian faith nor any other, but living without confessed religion at all. The dictionary reads this phenomenon by the light of Scripture, which knows no truly religionless man. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God—not a reasoned conclusion but a wish of the heart, for the creation declares its Maker and conscience accuses or excuses every man. Those without Christ are described by the apostle as having no hope, and without God in the world; yet they are not without worship, for the heart that will not bow to God bows to idols of its own making—self, pleasure, money, the state—hewing out broken cisterns that can hold no water in place of the fountain of living waters. The “none” is rarely a settled atheist; more often he is a man adrift, who has rejected the church but not slaked his thirst, religious about many things while confessing no religion. The dictionary names the “nones” not as a new category beyond the gospel’s reach but as the mission field at the church’s door: men and women made for God, restless until they rest in Him, to be met not with contempt but with the gospel that alone can fill the void their unbelief has left.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misjudgment to correct is the assumption that the “none” is truly without religion—a neutral, secular man who has simply outgrown faith. But Scripture knows no religionless heart. The man who confesses no religion still worships; having forsaken the fountain of living waters, he hews out broken cisterns—the idols of self, success, sex, ideology, the state—and pours his devotion there. Paul found even the philosophers of Athens religious, with an altar to an unknown god. The modern “none” is not empty of worship but disordered in it, adrift from the true God yet made for Him.

The principle to recover is the “nones” as a mission field, not a lost cause. They are men and women made in God’s image, restless until they rest in Him, often more aware of their thirst than the comfortable churchgoer. The church is not to despise them as beyond reach nor to flatter their unbelief, but to declare to them, as Paul declared the unknown God at Athens, the God they ignorantly seek and the Christ who alone can fill the void their unbelief has left. The same gospel that converted a pagan world can reach the “nones” of this one.

etymology: The title of Voddie Baucham’s 2021 critique of Critical Race Theory in the church; figuratively, the cracks along which a structure breaks.
biblical_def: Fault Lines is the title of a widely read 2021 book by the pastor Voddie Baucham, warning the church against the Critical Race Theory and so-called antiracism that had made deep inroads into evangelical institutions, and the phrase has come to name the danger of importing a worldly social framework into the gospel. The dictionary takes up the theme. Critical Race Theory and its antiracist offspring offer a rival anthropology and a rival gospel: they read the whole of human life through the lens of group power—oppressor and oppressed defined by race—substitute an unpayable, inherited group guilt for personal sin, and offer a salvation by ongoing activism rather than by the blood of Christ. This is another gospel, and the church that adopts it builds along a fault line that will crack. Scripture gives a wholly different account: all men are one in Adam, sharing one original sin, and those who believe are one in Christ, neither Jew nor Greek, all one in Him. The ministry of reconciliation is committed to the church through the cross, not through the categories of critical theory; and the LORD requires that we do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly—real justice, not the partial justice of group vengeance. The dictionary names CRT and its antiracism as a competing worldview to be refused, and pleads for the true unity and true justice that are found only in the gospel of the one Adam and the one Christ.

corruption_summary: Critical Race Theory and antiracism are smuggled into the church as justice; they are a rival anthropology of inherited group guilt and salvation by activism, answered by oneness in Adam and in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is Critical Race Theory and the antiracism that flows from it, pressed upon the church as the demand of justice. This framework reads the whole of human life through the single lens of group power—dividing mankind into oppressor and oppressed by race—and so functions as a rival worldview to the gospel. It replaces personal sin with an inherited, collective, race-based guilt that can never be repented of or removed; it replaces justification by the blood of Christ with an endless salvation-by-activism; and it makes group identity, not the imago Dei and union with Christ, the deepest truth about a person. Imported into the church, it is another gospel, and it builds along a fault line that will surely crack.

The principle to recover is the biblical account of man: one in Adam and one in Christ. All men share one nature and one original sin, for by one man sin entered the world and death passed upon all; and all who believe are one in Christ, in whom there is neither Jew nor Greek, bond nor free. The church’s answer to real injustice is not the partial justice of group vengeance but the true justice the LORD requires—to do justly, love mercy, and walk humbly—and the ministry of reconciliation given through the cross. Sin is personal, guilt is not inherited by skin, and reconciliation is by the blood of Christ, not the categories of critical theory.

etymology: American author (b. 1974) of I Kissed Dating Goodbye, who later renounced his book, his ministry, and the Christian faith.
biblical_def: Joshua Harris is the American author who, as a young man in the 1990s, wrote the enormously popular courtship book I Kissed Dating Goodbye and pastored a prominent church, and who in 2019 publicly renounced his book, announced the end of his marriage, and declared that he was no longer a Christian. The dictionary records his story soberly, not to mock a man but to learn from a warning. The case illustrates the difference between a profession of faith and the possession of it, and the bitter end of public deconstruction. Scripture is plain that not all who are numbered with the church are truly of it: they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us. The seed sown on stony ground springs up quickly and withers when tribulation or persecution arises, having no root in itself. The just shall live by faith, but the soul that draws back, God’s soul has no pleasure in; and no man, having put his hand to the plough and looking back, is fit for the kingdom. The dictionary names Harris’s apostasy as a grief and a caution: a reminder that early influence and even genuine-seeming ministry are no substitute for a root in Christ, that perseverance to the end is the mark of true grace, and that the church must build her young not on the latest movement but on the unchanging gospel.

corruption_summary: Public “deconstruction” is celebrated as honesty and growth; Scripture names the falling away of one who had no root as apostasy, and holds that perseverance is the mark of true grace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the celebration of public deconstruction—the renouncing of the faith paraded as a brave and healthy journey of growth, the apostate honored for his honesty. Harris’s public departure was widely praised in just these terms. But Scripture will not call apostasy maturity. The falling away of one who once professed and even ministered is not enlightenment but the manifesting of a faith that had no root; they went out from us because they were not of us. To rebrand abandonment of Christ as authenticity is to flatter the very ruin of a soul.

The principle to recover is perseverance as the mark of true grace and the necessity of a root in Christ. Genuine faith endures; the just shall live by faith, and the soul that draws back, God has no pleasure in. The seed on stony ground springs up fast and withers fast, having no root; early popularity, a bestselling book, even a pastorate, are no substitute for being truly rooted in Christ. The dictionary records Harris’s case not to despair—for God can yet recover the wanderer—but as a solemn caution to build the young on the unchanging gospel, and to pray that profession may prove to be possession, persevering to the end.

etymology: American pastor (1934–1997), founder of the Vineyard movement and popularizer of “power evangelism” and the “Third Wave.”
biblical_def: John Wimber was the American pastor who founded the Association of Vineyard Churches and became the chief popularizer of what was called the “Third Wave” of the charismatic movement, teaching “power evangelism”—the claim that signs, wonders, healings, prophecy, and words of knowledge should accompany the preaching of the gospel as its ordinary demonstration of divine power. The dictionary grants what may be granted: a zeal for evangelism, a desire to see God glorified, and a reaction against a dead and merely intellectual religion. But it cannot commend Wimber’s teaching, which the cessationist conviction of the dictionary judges to be in error. The promise of accompanying signs and wonders for every believer sets a fallible “word from the Lord” alongside the sufficient Scripture, loads tender souls with false expectations of guaranteed healing, and opens the door to the testing of doctrine by experience rather than experience by doctrine. The Lord warned that many would say in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in Thy name and done many wonderful works, only to be told He never knew them; that false prophets would show great signs and wonders; and that the spirits must be tried whether they are of God. God is not the author of confusion. The dictionary names Wimber’s power-evangelism as a corruption of the sufficiency of Scripture and the cessation of the sign-gifts, while distinguishing the sober desire for God’s power from the unwarranted promise of continuing miracles.

corruption_summary: Power-evangelism promises continuing signs, wonders, and prophecy for every believer; the dictionary’s cessationism answers that the sign-gifts ceased and the spirits must be tried by the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the “power evangelism” Wimber popularized—the teaching that miraculous signs, healings, words of knowledge, and prophecy are the ordinary, expected accompaniment of gospel preaching today. This errs on several heads. It sets a fallible contemporary “word from the Lord” alongside the all-sufficient Scripture, eroding the closed canon; it burdens the suffering with false promises of guaranteed healing and then with false guilt when healing does not come; and it trains the church to judge truth by experience rather than experience by the Word. The Lord warned that wonders prove nothing of themselves—false prophets show great signs, and many who prophesied and worked wonders in His name will hear, I never knew you.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Scripture, the cessation of the sign-gifts, and the trying of every spirit by the Word. God is not the author of confusion but of peace; the believer is commanded not to believe every spirit but to try the spirits whether they are of God, the test being conformity to the Scripture once delivered. The dictionary distinguishes a sober longing for God’s power in the salvation of sinners—which is good—from the unwarranted promise of continuing miracles, which is error. The power of God unto salvation is the gospel itself, and the church lives by the written Word, not by signs and wonders.

etymology: The great frontier camp meeting at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, in August 1801; a high point of the Second Great Awakening.
biblical_def: The Cane Ridge Revival was the enormous frontier camp meeting held at Cane Ridge in Bourbon County, Kentucky, in August 1801, when thousands—by some estimates ten to twenty thousand—gathered for days of preaching, prayer, and the Lord’s Supper, in one of the most dramatic episodes of the Second Great Awakening on the American frontier. The dictionary weighs it with discernment, neither dismissing nor uncritically praising. Where the Word was preached and sinners were truly pricked in their heart, brought to repentance, and gathered into the churches, there the Spirit of God was at work, and the longing of the psalmist—wilt thou not revive us again, that thy people may rejoice in thee?—was answered. True revival is the Spirit’s sovereign quickening, and the new birth is His secret work, like the wind that bloweth where it listeth. Yet Cane Ridge was also marked by physical excesses—falling, jerking, barking, uncontrolled outcry—and by a feverish emotionalism that sober observers, then and since, judged to be the work of crowd and flesh rather than of the Spirit. The dictionary holds that genuine revival bears the fruit of repentance, faith, and holiness under the Word, and is to be distinguished from mere emotional contagion; for God is not the author of confusion, but of peace. Cane Ridge is read, then, as a true work of God attended by the disorder of the flesh: to be received where it bowed men to Christ, and tested where it gave way to excess.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the discerning of true revival from its counterfeit. Cane Ridge has been claimed both by those who would dismiss all awakening as mere frontier hysteria and by those who would canonize every excess as the Spirit’s work. The dictionary refuses both. The physical phenomena—the falling, jerking, and barking—and the feverish emotionalism were not the measure of the Spirit’s presence, and later revivalism’s error was to make such excitement the goal and to manufacture it by technique and pressure. God is not the author of confusion; where disorder and the contagion of crowds replaced the sober preaching of the Word, the flesh was at work.

The principle to recover is true revival as the Spirit’s sovereign quickening, known by its fruit. Where the Word was preached and men were pricked in their heart, brought to repentance and faith, and gathered into the churches in lasting holiness, there God was truly at work—and the church does well to pray, wilt thou not revive us again? The new birth is the Spirit’s secret work, like the wind that bloweth where it listeth; it cannot be worked up by men. Genuine revival is tested not by the intensity of feeling but by the fruit of repentance, sound doctrine, and a holy life under the Word.

etymology: The false notion that faith is belief without or against evidence; the “blind faith” caricature pressed by modern skeptics.
biblical_def: Faith against evidence is the false definition of faith—urged by the new atheists and assumed by much of the age—as believing without evidence, or even against the evidence; a leap in the dark, a credulity opposed to reason. The dictionary rejects this caricature as a slander on biblical faith. The faith Scripture commends is not believing without grounds but trusting the trustworthy God on the strongest of grounds—His own testimony, confirmed by His mighty works. The risen Lord did not commend Thomas’s doubt but met it with evidence: reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; be not faithless, but believing. The apostles rested the faith on witnessed fact: He showed Himself alive after His passion by many infallible proofs. John wrote his Gospel that men might believe upon the evidence recorded: these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ. And the believer is commanded to be ready always to give an answer—a reasoned defense—to every man that asks a reason of the hope that is in him. Biblical faith is not contrary to reason but reasonable trust in the God who has spoken and acted in history; its certainty rests not on the strength of the believer’s wishing but on the faithfulness of the One believed. The dictionary names “faith against evidence” as a corruption of the biblical idea, answered by a faith grounded in the testimony of God and the witnessed resurrection of His Son.

corruption_summary: Skeptics define faith as believing without or against evidence; biblical faith is reasonable trust in the God who has testified and acted, grounded in His Word and the witnessed resurrection of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to answer is the skeptic’s redefinition of faith as belief without evidence, or against it—the “blind faith” the new atheists set up to knock down, treating all believing as a willful credulity opposed to reason. But this is a caricature, not the faith of Scripture. The Bible never asks men to believe against the evidence; it grounds faith in the testimony of God and the witnessed acts of God in history. To define faith as the enemy of evidence is to fight a straw man and to slander the reasonable trust the Scriptures everywhere commend.

The principle to recover is biblical faith as reasonable trust in the trustworthy God. The risen Christ rebuked Thomas’s unbelief not by demanding a leap in the dark but by showing His wounds; He proved Himself alive by many infallible proofs; the Gospels were written that men might believe upon the recorded evidence; and believers are charged to give a reasoned answer for their hope. Faith is not contrary to reason but rests on the surest of grounds—the God who cannot lie, who has spoken in His Word and acted in raising His Son. Its assurance lies not in the strength of the believer’s wishing but in the faithfulness of the One in whom he trusts.
